slides.texte_overlay:
Habits that make you
disgustingly articulate
Read out loud for five minutes a day. A book, an article, anything. It trains your mouth to keep up with your brain, and after a few weeks you'll stumble over words a lot less in real life.
Replace "like" and "um" with a pause. When you feel a filler word coming, just stop for half a second. Silence sounds thoughtful. Fillers make even smart ideas sound unsure.
Learn one new word a week and use it three times. Not fancy words, precise ones. "Reluctant" instead of "didn't really want to." Precision is what makes people sound sharp.
Make your point first, explain second. "I think we should leave at six. Traffic gets bad after that." Leading with the point makes you sound clear. Building up to it makes people lose interest.
Tell stories in three parts. What happened, what went wrong, how it ended. Practice once on a friend. Structured stories are easy to follow, and people remember the guy who tells them well.
Ask yourself "What do I actually mean?" before you text or speak in a meeting. Cut the first half of what you were going to say. Most people talk too long before they get to the point.
Feed your vocabulary every day. Five minutes of history, art or science and you'll pick up words and ideas nobody around you uses. Articulate people are curious people.
slides.texte_sophia: Before: "it was, like, really good, you know?" After: five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. New words and ideas, every single day.
